question: Which candidate inference algorithm, if any, do pretrained language models actually use when predicting synthetic hidden-Markov sequences in context, and can an algorithmic representation be shown to be both decodable from and causally used by their residual streams?

key_findings.claim: Across the authors' HMM sweep, no one classical baseline matches pretrained-LLM behavior at all contexts and regimes, although finite-window n-gram and spectral families each match subsets of the behavior.
key_findings.evidence: Twelve untuned open-weight models are compared with oracle forward recursion, spectral moment methods, linear and nonlinear n-grams, and Baum-Welch on 75 configurations and context lengths 4-4096. The detailed appendix reports different regime- and length-dependent matches rather than one winner.

key_findings.claim: Baum-Welch is behaviorally inconsistent with the gradual in-context learning curve of the tested LLMs, despite being a strong predictor.
key_findings.evidence: With the hidden-state count supplied, ten random restarts, and up to 200 EM iterations, Baum-Welch achieves high accuracy at short contexts and remains comparatively stable; LLMs generally improve gradually with context. The authors therefore rule out this explicit iterative parameter-estimation mechanism among their candidates.

anchors.section: 2.3 No single algorithm explains LLM behavior

key_findings.claim: For known HMM parameters, a finite-window next-observation probability can be written as a linear function of a Kronecker n-gram feature, and additive and Kronecker features are linked by linear and ReLU maps.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.1 constructs q_{t+1}=G_{t,n} phi_t^(n), where phi is the tensor product of the last n one-hot observations. A fixed linear map takes phi to the stacked additive feature psi, while a ReLU threshold of a linear map recovers phi from psi. The operator G_{t,n} is time dependent through the earlier belief and normalization.

anchors.section: C.1 Nonlinear Features for n-gram Prediction
C.2 Linear Features for n-gram Prediction

key_findings.claim: Idealized Transformer constructions can assemble finite-window features and emulate full-batch logistic-regression gradient descent in logarithmic depth under a logarithmic iteration budget.
key_findings.evidence: One construction assigns n heads to n lags; another uses a binary tree of tensor products in O(log n) layers. After matching the query history, attention aggregates its count and label statistics, and repeated MLP blocks approximate GD updates. Total depth is O(log n+T), hence O(log n) when T=O(log n).

anchors.section: Lemma C.6 and C.5 Transformer can Implement Gradient Descent

key_findings.claim: The paper also assembles prior primitives into an O(log(n+m))-depth capability construction for spectral HMM prediction.
key_findings.evidence: Empirical unigram, bigram, and trigram operators are decomposed into attention-compatible primitives. Neumann iterations approximate the projected inverse, prior n-gram constructions estimate trigram action, and a prior binary-tree composition applies observation operators without materializing each matrix.

anchors.section: Approximating the spectral primitives and composition

key_findings.claim: A small Transformer trained on sequences from one fixed HMM learns a short recent-context mechanism rather than the general in-context spectral construction.
key_findings.evidence: With 8,000 length-2,049 sequences split evenly between train and validation, one layer, one head, width 64, and FFN width 256 suffice; deeper models do not improve materially and smaller dimensions underfit. Attention concentrates on recent tokens, and the discrepancy from a finite-window theoretical predictor converges around window length six.

anchors.section: 3.2 Which Algorithm does a Small Trained Transformer use?

key_findings.claim: The small Transformer's post-attention representation is primarily additive even though its output behaves like the nonlinear tabular n-gram predictor.
key_findings.evidence: Across window sizes, output cosine similarity to the Kronecker predictor is about 1.0 while similarity to the additive predictor falls to about 0.97. In the post-attention residual, alignment reverses: additive mapping approaches 0.95 and Kronecker mapping saturates near 0.76 once K^n exceeds width 64. The authors infer that attention routes lagged one-hots and the MLP performs the nonlinear lift.

anchors.section: E.4 Linear vs. Kronecker n-gram Feature Mappings

key_findings.claim: Principal Activations Probe separates linear decodability from causal use by combining a low-rank PCA-ridge probe with three increasingly targeted activation patches.
key_findings.evidence: For each layer, PAP regresses an algorithm state from the top k activation PCs and evaluates held-out MSE and R-squared. It then compares full-residual replacement, PCA-subspace replacement, and a minimum-norm probe-inverse perturbation, measuring KL to the target algorithmic distribution and interchange-intervention accuracy.

anchors.section: 4.1 Principal Activations Probe and Causal Intervention

key_findings.claim: Bayes-optimal belief is linearly decodable from Qwen3-1.7B residuals, but high probe quality can occur at layers where even an unrestricted residual patch has no causal effect.
key_findings.evidence: For a three-state example, k=9 gives high R-squared in early and late layers and k=243 is near perfect from layer one onward. In the slow-mixing, noisy-emission regime, layers 0-2 have high belief-probe R-squared while full, PCA, and inverse patches fail to steer output. OLMo-2-1B supplies a model-level counterexample: high belief R-squared but full-residual intervention fails entirely.

key_findings.claim: The causal effect of candidate states is regime dependent, with a soft n-gram representation the most consistently effective of those tested.
key_findings.evidence: Bigram is highly decodable in both the belief- and observation-dominated regimes, but its patch is nearly inert when long-context belief tracking is needed and strongly steering when the latest observation nearly identifies state. Linear/soft n-gram patching is stronger than bigram or spectral in the belief-dominated case and all three are effective in the observation-dominated case.

anchors.section: 4.3 The model recruits different representations across regimes
G.5-G.6 Additional intervention and belief results

key_findings.claim: Where a candidate state exerts stronger causal influence, the LLM's output distribution also converges to that candidate sooner in the two highlighted regimes.
key_findings.evidence: In the belief-dominated example, the LLM converges to the linear n-gram by position 64 while bigram and spectral remain behind through position 4096. In the observation-dominated example, all three reach the oracle by position 1024, matching their broader causal-patching effects.

anchors.section: Figure 13 Causal representation quality predicts empirical performance

key_findings.claim: Most oracle-belief probe performance saturates in a 64-128-dimensional principal subspace, while harder emission regimes require more directions and middle layers distribute the information more diffusely.
key_findings.evidence: Across nine entropy configurations and k from 4 to 2048, the appendix reports little probe improvement beyond about 64-128 PCs. Low-rank probes are weakest in middle layers, and higher emission entropy shifts saturation to larger k.

anchors.section: G.4 Quality at Varying top-k Principal Components

key_findings.claim: Prediction-relevant belief is concentrated at the current token but can also be causally accumulated across several preceding positions in harder regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Full-residual window patches that include the query nearly completely transfer prediction even at n=1. Excluding the query makes n=1 almost inert, while preceding windows of length 4-6 become effective at later layers and times, especially under high emission entropy.

key_findings.claim: Natural-language pretraining can override the apparent simplicity of the synthetic task in an extreme repeated-token regime.
key_findings.evidence: When both transition and emission entropy are zero, the observation stream is a constant string that is theoretically trivial, yet most models fail to continue the repeated token. The authors attribute this to natural-language pretraining and exclude the configuration, leaving 74 for the subsequent failure analysis.

anchors.section: F.2 Cases When LLMs Fail to Converge to Oracle

method.core_idea: Triangulate an LLM's in-context algorithm using behavioral candidate matching, constructive capability results, and causal tests of candidate intermediate states rather than treating output similarity or probe decodability alone as identification.
method.mechanism: The study samples controlled HMM sequences while varying transition entropy, emission entropy, and observation alphabet. It compares restricted LLM next-token distributions with forward-oracle, Baum-Welch, spectral, linear n-gram, and nonlinear n-gram predictors using accuracy and Hellinger distance. Theoretical sections express HMM prediction through additive and tensor-product finite-window features and compile known Transformer primitives for feature construction, gradient descent, and spectral recursion. A small Transformer trained on one HMM tests which solution arises without language pretraining. For pretrained activations, PAP projects each layer's residuals onto top principal components, ridge-regresses a candidate belief or learned operator, and intervenes with full-residual, PCA-only, or probe-inverse patches. The final identification compares held-out decoding, causal steering, and behavioral convergence across HMM regimes.
assumptions: The main HMM family has four hidden states, stationary initialization, finite alphabets, and transition matrices selected to have real positive eigenvalues; most configurations are ergodic.
Normalized transition and emission entropies and alphabet size span the task factors relevant to an LLM's choice of prediction mechanism.
Mapping abstract observations to fixed vocabulary tokens and renormalizing logits over only those tokens elicits the intended HMM predictor rather than an uncontrolled token-specific language prior.
The benchmark candidate set is rich enough that agreement with soft n-gram, spectral, or belief states is informative about the operative computation.
Behavioral mismatch at short contexts can rule out Baum-Welch even if some implementation of iterative parameter estimation could be truncated, amortized, or initialized differently.
PAP train and test sequences come from the same HMM distribution, so decoding measures within-distribution representation rather than HMM-level generalization.
The leading variance directions contain the causally relevant algorithm state; low-variance nonlinear or distributed features may be missed.

Ridge probes map residual activations linearly to well-specified candidate states, and patching those directions does not create activation states so far off manifold that output changes become uninterpretable.

A shift toward the candidate's expected next-token distribution after patching is evidence that the model uses the represented candidate variable, although correlated candidate states can support similar interventions.
The capability proofs use identifiable positional encodings, ideal hard attention for exact routing or arbitrarily sharp softmax approximations, and MLP universal approximation for update maps.
The spectral construction can reuse accurately estimated low-order moments and an appropriate top-M singular subspace U throughout its binary composition.
The small fixed-HMM model is an architecture-level sanity check, not an in-context parameter-learning model, because it can memorize the shared HMM.

techniques.role: Varies state mixing, emission ambiguity, and observation aliasing independently across a structured synthetic test bed.
Converts pretrained next-token logits into a normalized distribution over the synthetic observation alphabet.
Compares accuracy, oracle distance, and baseline distance across context rather than naming an algorithm from one output curve.
Represents each finite observation suffix as a one-hot tensor-product feature so a tabular conditional predictor is linear in that feature.
Maps stacked lag one-hots to their Kronecker conjunction through a thresholding ReLU layer.
Uses multi-head lag selection or binary aggregation to collect and combine a length-n suffix.
Emulates logistic-regression GD only for the n-gram column matching the query instead of materializing the exponential table.
Decomposes observable-operator HMM inference into unigram aggregation, approximate inverse-bigram action, trigram action, and tree composition.
Fits layerwise PCA followed by ridge regression to decode candidate beliefs and learned operators from a controlled low-dimensional subspace.
Contrasts whole residual, top-PC, and minimum-norm probe-inverse interventions to distinguish accessibility from causal sufficiency.
Measures whether a source-target activation exchange transfers the discrete prediction associated with the target algorithm state.
Breaks belief-activation correspondence while preserving target marginals to test whether high held-out probe scores reflect genuine alignment.
Separates belief stored at the readout token from information distributed over preceding positions.
Treats high probe accuracy without successful intervention as negative evidence for operational use.

evaluations.setting: 75 HMM configurations with M=4, transition and emission entropy each in {0,.25,.5,.75,1}, N in {2,4,8}; 4,096 sequences per configuration
evaluations.metric: Top-1 accuracy, Hellinger-to-oracle, and Hellinger-to-baseline at contexts 4-4096
evaluations.result: No one baseline matches all 12 LLMs across regimes and lengths; n-gram and spectral candidates each match subsets
evaluations.baseline: Bayes forward oracle, two spectral variants, three linear n-gram variants, two nonlinear n-gram variants, and Baum-Welch

evaluations.metric: Accuracy and Hellinger trajectories over context length

limitations: Author-stated: the empirical study is restricted to synthetic HMMs with small finite state and observation alphabets.
Author-stated: linear probing limits conclusions about nonlinear or distributed representations, and the analysis is layer-level rather than head-, neuron-, or circuit-level.
Author-stated by design: the small trained Transformer sees one fixed HMM and can memorize its parameters, so it does not demonstrate general-purpose in-context HMM learning.
Author-stated through results: no single candidate explains behavior in all regimes; the final soft-n-gram identification is a best-supported approximation, not exact recovery of one program.
Reviewer-identified: the 12-model behavioral breadth is not matched mechanistically; principal causal results use Qwen3-1.7B, with Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2-1B providing narrower checks.

Reviewer-identified: candidate states are statistically correlated and can imply similar next-token distributions, so successful patching of a soft n-gram state does not uniquely exclude an untested algorithm carrying the same sufficient statistic.

Reviewer-identified: PAP is within-distribution by construction; random train/test sequence splits from one HMM do not test whether a decoded operator generalizes to new transition or emission matrices.
Reviewer-identified: PCA privileges high-variance directions and ridge probes only linear readouts. A causal state encoded nonlinearly, sparsely, or in low-variance directions can be missed.

Reviewer-identified: activation replacement and pseudoinverse perturbations may be off manifold. A failed patch can reflect downstream error correction or invalid activations, and a successful patch can propagate correlated token identity as well as the intended algorithm state.

Reviewer-identified: the conclusion that LLMs do not implement statistically optimal iterative inference is stronger than ruling out the tested Baum-Welch configuration and finding finite-window correlates; amortized, truncated, or hybrid iterative procedures remain possible.

Reviewer-identified: the exact finite-window operator G_{t,n} in Lemma 3.1 depends on earlier belief and normalization. Treating prediction as one stationary linear regression on the last n observations requires additional mixing or approximation conditions.

Reviewer-identified: Kronecker feature dimension and corresponding tabular sample complexity grow exponentially in n; the query-only construction avoids materializing all columns but does not remove rare-suffix data scarcity.

Reviewer-identified: theoretical constructions establish capability, not what pretrained weights compute. They use exact lag routing, hard-attention idealizations or arbitrarily sharp softmax, universal MLP approximation, and a logarithmic GD-iteration assumption.

Reviewer-identified: the spectral construction assumes an appropriate SVD subspace and stable inverse/moment estimates, then compiles prior primitives; it gives no finite-width, finite-precision, or sample-error bound for the resulting Transformer.
Reviewer-identified: most intervention conclusions are shown as heatmaps without numerical summaries, seed variation, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests.
Reviewer-identified: fixed vocabulary mappings introduce a confound demonstrated by the zero-entropy constant-string failure, yet token-map sensitivity is not systematically ablated.
Reviewer-identified: the code is not available at submission; the checklist promises release only upon acceptance.

Reviewer-identified reproducibility contradiction: the checklist says training details and compute resources are supplied, but the extraction contains no optimizer, learning rate, hardware, memory, runtime, or total-compute description for the small-model and PAP experiments.

Reviewer-identified statistical-reporting contradiction: the checklist marks significance as addressed because ridge regression is closed form, but closed-form fitting does not quantify variability of LLM comparisons, probe scores, or interventions and the paper reports no error-bar method.
Reviewer-identified setup contradiction: the main text describes the small trained HMM as M=N=3, while Appendix E.1 describes three states and twelve observations for the architecture ablation.
Reviewer-identified notation/error concern: Appendix G.2 calls 4.18 a mixing rate even though the paper defines mixing rate in [0,1); this is likely an uncorrected label or numerical typo.

Reviewer-identified intervention-description ambiguity: the main PAP description patches a source run with target information, whereas Appendix G.9 describes overwriting a target residual with source residuals; pair symmetry may preserve the experiment, but source/target metric conventions should be explicit.
failure_modes: A repeated observation token can trigger natural-language repetition priors and make a trivial deterministic HMM harder for the LLM than a noisy one.
At high emission entropy, a short n-gram discards older observations that materially improve latent-state belief, so finite-window predictions remain suboptimal.
At large alphabet size or window order, rare Kronecker suffixes receive too few examples for tabular or kernel n-gram estimation.
Spectral predictors become unstable when empirical bigram matrices are ill conditioned; the normalized variant avoids inversion at the cost of bias.

Baum-Welch can converge to poor local optima or behave differently with another initialization, hidden-state count, iteration cap, or online schedule, so one tuned batch version is not the whole iterative-inference class.
LLMs can degrade at very long prompts: Llama3.1-8B drops at length 4096 and OLMo shows a U-shaped trajectory at 1024-4096.
Probe R-squared can be misleading when the target state has low variance; the paper therefore pairs it with MSE, but visual interpretation can still overemphasize normalized scores.
A candidate variable may be linearly decodable in an early residual yet bypassed, overwritten, or ignored by later computation.
A full-residual patch can fail even for a decodable state if token identity, position, and other source features conflict with downstream circuitry.
A probe-inverse patch may exploit directions that satisfy the linear probe but do not correspond to any naturally occurring algorithm state.
Patching correlated beliefs can falsely favor one named algorithm when several predictors share the same next-token sufficient statistic.
PCA can exclude a low-variance causal direction and then make both the probe and targeted intervention falsely negative.
Nearest candidate matching by Hellinger distance can vary with context and regime, preventing a single discrete algorithm label.
The spectral Transformer construction can fail when moment error, pseudoinverse conditioning, or approximate softmax routing compounds through the recursive operator product.
The finite-window theoretical map becomes time or prefix dependent when the earlier belief has not mixed, undermining a single learned regression coefficient.
Layer-level localization can merge several distinct circuits that construct, transform, and read out the same algorithmic state.
reusable_insights: Algorithm identification should require agreement at three levels: input-output behavior, a realizable mechanistic hypothesis, and causal intervention on the hypothesis's intermediate state.
Always test decodability and causal use separately; a high-quality probe can identify information that downstream computation never reads.
Compare unrestricted residual replacement with subspace and probe-inverse patches so a targeted intervention is calibrated against the maximum effect available at that layer and position.
Use regimes in which candidate algorithms make different predictions or need different memory lengths; easy regimes can make all mechanisms observationally equivalent.
Factor sequence algorithms into routing and nonlinear feature formation: attention can gather lagged symbols while an MLP implements conjunctions or tensor-product lifts.
When an exponential feature table is one-hot, compute only the sufficient statistics for the query's active column rather than instantiate every column.
A current-token versus shifted-window intervention can measure whether a state is locally summarized or distributed across earlier context.
Behavioral edge cases that seem trivial can reveal strong pretraining priors and should be reported rather than silently averaged away.
Probe both dynamic beliefs and slowly changing learned operators; they distinguish state tracking from in-context parameter estimation.
Use label-shuffled probes and same-distribution held-out splits as minimum controls, then add HMM-level distribution shifts for stronger algorithm claims.
Interpret capacity constructions as possibility proofs and trained-model interventions as use evidence; neither substitutes for the other.
open_questions: Does PAP identify the same causal state under counterfactual transition/emission matrices held out at the HMM level rather than only new sequences from one HMM?
Can nonlinear or sparse causal probes find representations missed by top-variance PCA without making interventions less interpretable?
How sensitive are the behavior and patching conclusions to the arbitrary mapping from HMM observations to vocabulary tokens?
Can circuit-level analysis distinguish attention heads that collect lagged observations from MLPs that form nonlinear n-gram interactions in a pretrained LLM?
What hybrid or amortized iterative algorithms remain consistent with the same soft-n-gram beliefs and causal patches?
Can interventions target operator estimates rather than only beliefs and show that changing an inferred transition rule generalizes across future positions?
How does effective context length scale with HMM mixing time, emission entropy, alphabet size, and model scale under controlled error bars?
What on-manifold causal intervention can change one candidate algorithm state while holding token identity and correlated candidate states fixed?
Can the theoretical spectral and GD constructions be made finite-width with explicit approximation and sample-complexity bounds?
Why do OLMo models and some long-context Llama runs degrade, and does the failure arise from positional encoding, repetition priors, or a different algorithmic state?
Would natural-language latent-state tasks show the same early-decodable/late-causal stage separation?
Can a preregistered numeric summary of IIA and KL across seeds replace visual heatmap judgments and establish statistically reliable algorithm rankings?

competitive_landscape.title: Pre-trained Large Language Models Learn to Predict Hidden Markov Models In-context
competitive_landscape.difference: Dai et al. previously established the behavioral phenomenon that pretrained LLM predictions approach HMM Bayes-optimal posteriors and compared classical baselines. The present work starts from that result, broadens the controlled candidate comparison, adds constructive links among candidate algorithms, and most importantly probes and intervenes on their internal states; the original discovery of HMM ICL is not new here.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry in their Residual Stream
competitive_landscape.difference: Shai et al. show that next-token-predicting Transformers on hidden-state processes linearly represent fractal belief-state geometry in residual activations. This paper reproduces that geometry in pretrained LLMs but adds named algorithm candidates, learned-operator probes, and causal activation interventions demonstrating that belief decodability and use can diverge.

competitive_landscape.title: On Limitation of Transformer for Learning HMMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Hu et al. analyze Transformer representation limits and constructions for HMM learning, including the binary-tree machinery reused by this paper's spectral implementation. The current work compiles those capability results with finite-window and GD constructions and tests actual pretrained residual states; it does not replace Hu et al.'s representational theory with a new lower-bound analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Hao et al. explain HMM in-context learning through feature decoupling in a multi-task theoretical model. This paper instead compares multiple concrete algorithm families against open pretrained LLMs and uses causal residual interventions; its evidence favors regime-dependent finite-window statistics rather than identifying one decoupling theorem as the operative algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning In-context n-grams with Transformers: Sub-n-grams are Near-stationary Points
competitive_landscape.difference: Varre et al. derive how Transformers learn n-gram statistics and provide attention constructions reused for trigram estimation here. The present paper extends n-grams to HMM candidate identification, contrasts them with spectral and belief algorithms, and supplies pretrained-model probing and patching; the core n-gram learning mechanism and relevant construction predate it.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention with Markov: A Curious Case of Single-layer Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Makkuva et al. characterize how single-layer Transformers learn Markov-chain prediction and induction-like statistics when observations are states. This paper studies partially observed HMMs, where emission ambiguity can require belief integration, and uses that regime contrast to separate bigram-like behavior from richer soft n-grams and spectral candidates.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: the paper closes the algorithm-identification gap for pretrained-LLM HMM prediction with a three-stage pipeline, introduces PAP, and concludes that finite-window gradient-descent-like soft n-gram statistics rather than statistically optimal iterative inference causally drive prediction in a regime-dependent way. Reviewer inference: the strongest defensible novelty is not the prior behavioral discovery, belief-state geometry, Transformer implementability, or n-gram construction. It is the integrated candidate-specific PAP protocol—especially comparing full, PCA-subspace, and probe-inverse interventions—and the empirical dissociations between decodability and causal use across layers, HMM regimes, and one poorly performing model. The evidence narrows the operative sufficient statistics toward soft n-grams but does not uniquely extract an algorithm: candidates are incomplete and correlated, interventions may be off manifold, most causal evidence centers on one model, and Baum-Welch mismatch does not eliminate all iterative or hybrid inference. The work is therefore a substantial causal-diagnostic advance with a narrower algorithm-recovery claim than the title and conclusion suggest.
reviewer_notes: The complete 83-page extraction was inspected, including the main text, constructive proofs, small-model ablations, all behavioral/PAP appendices, figure captions, null test, window patches, references, and NeurIPS checklist. Six primary arXiv/OpenReview records were independently checked as direct prior or competing work. Explicit inconsistencies retained: main text M=N=3 versus Appendix E's three states/twelve observations for the small model; a reported mixing rate of 4.18 despite the defined [0,1) range; and checklist claims of complete optimizer/compute/significance reporting despite no such resource or uncertainty details in the extraction. The main and G.9 sections also reverse source/target patch wording. These lower reproducibility confidence, not the qualitative evidence that decodability and causal use differ.
